question: On 9 July 2026, Parliament failed to reject the Council’s position extending the ‘Chat Control 1.0’ system, established by Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, until 2028. It adopted amendments excluding end-to-end encrypted communications. The scanning of all other communications was retained on a voluntary basis for the provider, but not for the user, whose communications are analysed without any suspicion of a crime.

In Opinion 7/2026 concerning this system, the European Data Protection Supervisor highlighted the lack of a clear legal basis and safeguards against blanket scanning. ‘Chat Control 2.0’ (COM(2022) 209) -– which will feature orders to detect content – is currently in the pipeline. 1.

How does the Commission explain the compatibility of scanning the communications of persons not under suspicion with Articles 7, 8 and 52(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, as well as the case-law of the CJEU concerning the limits of general and indiscriminate interference with the confidentiality of communications – in particular the Digital Rights Ireland and La Quadrature du Net judgments – especially given that the scanning covers the content of messages?

On what evidence does the Commission base the effectiveness and proportionality of Chat Control 1.0, given that in report COM(2025) 740 it acknowledged that the data do not provide grounds to determine whether the system strikes a balance between combating child sexual exploitation and protecting users’ rights?

Will the Commission withdraw or amend the Chat Control 2.0 proposal so as to rule out the mass scanning of the communications of persons not under suspicion, interference with end-to-end encryption and the scanning of messages on the user’s device before they are encrypted?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.9.2026) The Commission Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse1 (‘the proposal’) is equipped with numerous specific protections and safeguards for the fundamental rights of the affected individuals.

The proposal relies on a thorough and publicly available impact assessment2, demonstrating that it strives to achieve a fair balance in the protection of the rights to respect privacy and protection of personal data and the rights of the child. In particular, detection orders are envisaged as measures of last resort when prevention measures are insufficient.

They are targeted only at services that are at risk, and at specific users or groups of users, where possible, and are issued by a judicial or independent administrative authority balancing all the rights at stake and following a thorough assessment of their necessity and proportionality. The proposal neither requires nor allows the indiscriminate scanning of private communications.

The implementation report3 finds that voluntary detection under Regulation (EU) 2021/12324 made a significant contribution to child protection: available data show that thousands of children were identified and millions of images and videos were removed from circulation, reducing secondary victimisation.

The Commission considers that the evidence supports the proportionality of the temporary and strictly limited regime, which remains justified to avoid legal gaps while negotiations on the proposed long-term Regulation continue. The Commission will continue to support interinstitutional negotiations.
The legislative process has advanced substantially, and the Commission is not aware of any reasons that would warrant withdrawing the proposal.
